entries.title: The Fire-Hose Style of Journalism: A Dirge for Salon
entries.summary: Salon wasn’t some programmer's hobby. It looked like a magazine, with zippy graphics and fonts. The prose was smart, stylish, amusing.
entries.content:
James Marcus

Document

In the dying days of 1995, I was a freelance journalist in Portland, Oregon, who spent most of my time seated at a rickety particle-board desk, a gift from my father-in-law. The desk was covered in faux-walnut laminate and swayed from side to side as I wrote. I had already finished my main financial gusher for that year, a history book for fifth graders, and I needed more work.

In this respect I was no different than any freelancer in literary history. In fact, the technology involved in my trade, and the speed at which it functioned—its industrial metabolism—had hardly changed in the preceding century. Of course, I had a computer. But it hardly seemed to be much more than a glorified typewriter. And of course I had an email account, courtesy of the nerd Valhalla known as CompuServe. But the business of freelance journalism was still built largely around stuffing wads of paper into envelopes and sending them to editors, who would then transform the contents into other wads of paper: newspapers, magazines, books. The product, whatever you thought of it, was palpable.

Into this cozy Victorian setting came an online publication called Salon. It had been launched that same fall by a crew of ex-staffers from the San Francisco Examiner, traditional journalists trying to break the mold. I don’t remember which Salon editor contacted me in the first place. I do remember reading the website in my chilly little office, steadying the stupid desk with one leg and feeling an almost metaphysical puzzlement. Salon wasn’t some programmer’s hobby, whipped up in creaky old COBOL. It looked like a magazine, with zippy graphics and respectable fonts. The prose was smart, stylish, and amusingly contrarian.

All of this made a kind of sense to me. What was tricky was that it was free. That first afternoon, I printed out one of the articles, about The Beatles Anthology, which was just then airing on TV. I suppose I was turning back the technological clock—transubstantiating the product back into paper. Reading Salon gratis made me feel as if I were doing something furtive, as though I were a shoplifter, but it represented a kind of post-Gutenberg freedom.

Over the next year, I would write many pieces for Salon. I started out with book reviews that were assigned to me by Dwight Garner. (He had previously edited a few things of mine at Vogue, in terms of ethos the absolute inverse of Salon and, eventually, in terms of finances too.) Dwight sent me books by the bushel, or so it felt. I wrote very short pieces for him very quickly; they appeared online almost immediately. This, for the journalist, was unprecedented and nearly beggared belief. No more waiting for your piece to come out, pacing the equivalent of a widow’s walk. Sometimes I was even instructed to send the piece straight to the copy editor so we could cut a few more minutes out of the process.

Speediness of reflexes was part of the value proposition for Salon. Within months, the “smart tabloid,” as its founder David Talbot called it, was posting daily rather than weekly. In this way it inaugurated a fire-hose style of journalism that would in time become universal. The new norm was not waiting, not allowing stories to lose their heat in the cooling saucer of classic media.

Salon’s politics were similarly nontraditional: left-leaning, libertarian-adjacent (as per its Bay Area digs), but without an obvious party line. It doubtless helped that the magazine was not a subsidiary of a larger corporation, which was the case with Slate (part of Microsoft) and the earlier, cruder Mr. Showbiz (part of Starwave, a short-lived multimedia platform founded by Microsoft’s Paul Allen). Yes, Salon’s seed funding had come from Apple—a mingy $60,000—followed by a more substantial disbursement to the tune of $2 million from the Adobe cofounder John Warnock and various other investors. But it was an independent entity, unconstrained by the need to tiptoe around the feelings of a corporate proprietor.

In any case, I wasn’t writing about politics. I was writing about culture: the magazine’s strong suit. From books I branched into music—I believe it was Joyce Millman, Salon’s television critic, who assigned me pieces about Prince, Los Lobos, Bill Frisell, Cassandra Wilson. These were my enthusiasms, not the sort of dutiful, indiscriminate coverage that a film-critic friend of mine once likened to servicing a vending machine. I was allowed to venture further still when I pitched a piece about Martin Scorsese’s use of music. (The Casino soundtrack, I wrote, struck me as what the director might listen to “if he were shipwrecked with nothing but a polyester suit and a bank of slot machines.”)

It wasn’t long before I was writing short personal essays. I wrote one about being hoaxed by the founder of the Church of Kurt Cobain, which turned out to be nonexistent, although certainly plausible in the drizzling, grunge-friendly atmosphere of Portland. I wrote another about becoming addicted to All My Children during a serious family health crisis in the midst of which I found myself strangely inspired by the surreal resiliency of the characters, who never died unless their respective actor’s contracts with the show expired. I’m not making any extreme claims for these pieces. They were written at the madcap pace dictated by Salon and sandwiched between other freelance explorations—of dental malocclusion or aluminum smelting, say. For me, though, they still evoke the adrenaline feel of the period, the wild sense of participating in something new and transformative.

Despite the constant flow of assignments from Salon, my paychecks, which still arrived by mail, were modest. About a year after I began writing for the website, and under continuing financial stress, I accepted a job offer from a tiny startup that I assumed would go bankrupt within a year: Amazon. I drove a diesel truck with all our belongings, minus the flimsy desk, up to Seattle. In a way, the nonstop sprint and kooky brevity of Salon had made for a kind of boot camp for what would follow at my new gig. You had to be fast, faster, fastest. Soon enough, I would be fending off the arguments of my Amazon supervisors that a 150-word book review was too long.

I hoped I might maintain my connection to the magazine, but Salon had entered into a sort of corporate dalliance with Borders. That made me a fifth-column traitor, just as it had when the New York Times Book Review signed a similar deal with Barnes & Noble. (“I’m afraid you’re on the other team now,” my longtime editor at the Book Review explained during an awkward phone call.) Yet in 2004, by which time I had left Amazon and the retail mark of Cain had been washed from my forehead, Salon ran a long excerpt from my book Amazonia and paired it with an effusive review. Naturally, I hoped that the reviewer’s praise was sincere. But I also saw the attention as a tacit recognition of my earlier role at the magazine. I had stopped contributing, I had disappeared like one of those post-contractual players on All My Children—but I was still family, wasn’t I?

The downward trajectory of Salon, which closed its doors for good earlier this month, is well known. The magazine pioneered not only the rapidity and personality-driven prose of much modern journalism, but also its early hope that digital advertising would make up for the deficit left by giving away the product for free. This belief collapsed in due time. So did the nosebleed valuations of many enterprises during the dot-com boom. Salon was valued at $107 million when it went public in June 1999. (I can still recall one of the editors rejoicing to me on the phone: “We danced around the living room and said, ‘We’re rich, we’re rich!’”) Exactly two decades later, it sold for $5 million to a pair of entrepreneurs—who then passed it along for pocket change to a Malta-based “performance marketing ecosystem” whose website tilts powerfully toward cryptocurrency rather than journalism.

Who knows what the Maltese owners intended. A recent contributor remarked to me, “I suspect the crypto business that bought Salon always intended to drive it into the ground.” In the old days, this would have been insanity. Now it could be smart tax planning or a simple will to destruction of the sort much beloved by our current run of tech barons, whose creative enterprises so often require a mulch of wreckage underfoot. So Eden sank to grief!

And yet, the end of Salon (or of the dregs of Salon) is hard to contemplate. All these years later, with my disembodied pieces on the verge of vanishing, it feels like part of my youth, too, is dipping beneath the horizon. It seems to stir in me both fond recollection and an odd, head-scratching silence. What are the appropriate funeral rites? My plan is to hurriedly visit the archives, locate my work, and print it all out.

entries.title: My Whale Poem
entries.summary: “In 2026, I noticed people discussing my poem on X. Pangram had identified it as 100 percent AI-generated.”
entries.content:
I wrote this in February 2005, when I was twenty-one:

i went fishing with my family when i was five

when i was five

i went fishing with my family

my dad caught a turtle

my mom caught a snapper

my brother caught a crab

i caught a whale

that night we ate crab

the next night we ate turtle

the next night we ate snapper

the next night we ate whale

the next night we ate whale

the next night we ate whale

…

The first draft repeated the last line 143 times. I sent it to an editor at Monkeybicycle—an online literary magazine—and he accepted it for publication. He wrote:

The average weight of a small sea turtle is 60 lbs. The largest whale (the Blue Whale) averages 120 tons. So, that’s 4000 times larger. I was thinking we could repeat the final line 4000 times.

I emailed the poem to my mom, who replied, “Children would enjoy it very much, what do you think? Maybe sometimes you can write something for children someday. Just have a question, there are several hundred lines of ‘the next night we ate whale,’ is it supposed to be like that or it is a mistake? I tried to delete it, but couldn’t.”

The Monkeybicycle editor sent me his 24,059-word file of the poem and suggested I find an illustrator and publish it as “a huge chapbook.” Another Monkeybicycle editor said he’d illustrate and lay it out, but I wasn’t interested.

I read the poem at readings maybe five or six times. I remember staying focused and serious while reading it by dwelling on how depressed and alienated I felt. The longest I ever read it was seven minutes, I think.

In 2008, my friend recorded a video of the audience as I read the poem. This video is on YouTube. I began the reading by saying, “I’m going to read from my memoir.” Afterward, I sold stapled booklets of a short version of the poem for three dollars.

In 2009, I was paid a hundred dollars to read the poem for four minutes at the New Museum of Contemporary Art. In 2010, the London Review of Books published an overview of my writing career that referenced the poem, and someone read the poem at a cultural center in Amsterdam. Also in 2010, at an event at Drawn & Quarterly’s bookstore for my second novel, I pitched the poem as a book to D&Q’s owner. I described this in my novel Taipei (2013): 

… the owner of Drawn & Quarterly approached and thanked Paul for coming to Montreal. Paul pitched a children’s book, to be illustrated by a known graphic novelist who’d confirmed interest, based on one of his poems—

when i was five i went fishing with my family

when i was five

i went fishing with my family

my dad caught a turtle

my mom caught a snapper

my brother caught a crab

i caught a whale

that night we ate crab

the next night we ate turtle

the next night we ate snapper

the next night we ate whale

the next night we ate whale

the next night we ate whale

the next night we ate whale

the next night we ate whale

the next night we ate whale

—with each line on its own page and the last line repeated as many times as needed. Maybe a different artist could illustrate each page to create a sort of anthology. As a children’s book, due to the content, it would …

The owner didn’t seem interested.

In 2012, the Asian American Writer’s Workshop asked me to participate in an event. The organization suggested four things I could do. The first was to read the whale poem. I chose another option. I was tired of reading the poem.

In 2013, I got an email that said, “The Head of English at the University of Exeter just randomly sent everyone on the Poetry module a video of you reading ‘i went fishing with my family when i was five’ as an example of how poetry isn’t dull.”

In 2014, Jeffrey Brown, the author of Clumsy (2002), one of my favorite graphic novels, agreed to illustrate my whale poem. An editor at McSweeney’s was interested in it for their children’s-book imprint. But this didn’t result in anything.

I mostly stopped caring about making the poem into a book. Sometimes people messaged me saying they’d performed it at a reading. A band used it as lyrics for a song. A doctoral student at Oxford used it as the text for a composition that the BBC Singers—a professional chamber choir—performed in a workshop setting.

In 2026, I noticed people discussing my poem on X. Pangram had identified it as 100 percent AI-generated. It was the only false positive discovered in a public challenge offering $4,100 to find one from before 2020 that was longer than 749 words.

This gave my poem more attention than it had ever gotten, encouraging me to make and publish the book myself. I handwrote, illustrated, and designed it over a week. I loved the process.

From i went fishing with my family when i was five, published today by Muumuu House.

Tao Lin is the author of the novels Leave Society and Taipei, among other books. His poetry collection Hawaii Years is forthcoming from Louria Books. His most recent piece for the Daily was “Taiwan English.”

entries.title: Gurdjieff in the Golden State: The Mystic Haunting Joy Williams’s Fiction
entries.summary: “George Ivanovich Gurdjieff had—for me at least—everything to do with a small, neglected corner in the short fiction of Joy Williams.”
entries.content:
Drew Dickerson

Dispatch

My first mistake was to draw a connection. The flyers appeared all at once over the telephone poles of my neighborhood in the East Bay, with contact info provided on the kind of tear-away strips more typical of a HELP WANTED or FOR SALE notice, only here the subject read: AN INTRODUCTORY DISCUSSION: G. I. GURDJIEFF. The accompanying copy spoke of spiritual methods and cosmic scale; the words seemed to promise some tremendous synthesis between part and whole, spirit and matter, individual and collective. More prosaically, they advertised a series of public meetings to take place in Berkeley. My second mistake, I think, was to write an email expressing interest.

Where had I heard the name Gurdjieff? The question took me several minutes of standing in front of the poster to answer. I must have missed the crossing signal before remembering with a start that the life’s work of the Russian-born mystic, teacher, sacred choreographer, and occasional composer of piano music George Ivanovich Gurdjieff had—for me at least—everything to do with a small, neglected corner in the short fiction of Joy Williams.

“Gurdjieff in the Sunshine State” appears in Williams’s 1990 book Escapes, but is among the very few stories not to make it into her nearly comprehensive collection The Visiting Privilege, published twenty-five years later. I have never understood the logic behind its exclusion any more than I can claim to understand the story itself—in which G. astral projects to Florida, where, as a specter, he observes a roller rink, drinks a Tab, and chats briefly with what may be the ghost of Katherine Mansfield. By virtue of being disincluded from Williams’s collected work, this story of an esotericist feels in turn to have become itself esoteric, tucked away and little read. Even Williams’s own mentions of the story seemed charged with the force of mystery. “There is a Gurdjieff story in Escapes,” she wrote to her editor, the late Gary Fisketjon, in 2011. “I was going to write a whole mess of these stories on Gurdjieff but haven’t, you’re probably happy to know.”

*

The historical Gurdjieff was no stranger to hermetic situations. He traveled widely during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. In the course of his itinerary between the Mediterranean and southwest Asia, he absorbed the teachings that would result in his syncretistic blend of Sufi, Hindu, Zen, and Christian tendencies. But the articulation of his thought in a system and set of practices later known as the Fourth Way would come to be passed between generations, making Gurdjieff one of the most influential figures in what we today call the New Age Movement.

Some of this biographical picture was imparted at the first public meeting I attended in the auxiliary room of a Unitarian Universalists Fellowship Hall. For practical purposes the scene might have been lifted straight out of the fiction of Williams herself—from “The Country,” say, in which a group of denominationally wide-ranging seekers meet weekly “in one of the many, many rooms” of an Episcopal church to discuss the question: “Why Are We Here?”

I took my seat in a circle of folding chairs under a framed black-and-white portrait of Gurdjieff that someone had arrived early to hang. It was the first time I’d seen a picture of him. His eyes were enormous. Introductory talk proceeded gnomically. Most present seemed to have been steeped in one or another Gurdjieff-adjacent current. All were capable of trading words as tokens in a kind of code I had trouble grasping.

“I was brought here out of interest in the work of Maurice Nicoll.”

“Yes, well. Nicoll certainly had a lot to say, didn’t he? Maybe he ran out of things to say by the time of his fifth book. You should read Ouspensky.”

“I’m wary of Ouspensky. Remember what Gurdjieff told him: if you understood half of what you know, you’d be my teacher.”

Why were we there? Newcomers were encouraged to share our answers to this question. I owned up to my literary detective work in tracking down this reference of Williams’s, so marginal in her body of work as to be secretive. I also said that I wanted to enjoy a closer relationship to God, which was true. 

Motivations varied. One woman mentioned a near-death experience several months ago that convinced her of the need for greater spiritual attunement. Another spoke about how, after a childhood spent being told to shut up, she was now emboldened to want to find her voice. Someone else detailed a fairly fresh LSD episode before producing a decorative knife that he told us had been forged from the metal of an authentic meteorite. The ceremonial blade looked no shorter than six inches.

Experience certainly struck me as a keyword in the group’s talk, in the sense of a spiritual experience’s spontaneous flash of insight that leaves one wholly changed. Vibration, too, was in frequent currency. Self-observation. Self-knowledge. Self-remembering. One first-time visitor’s chancing upon the term wish was met with a gasp. The wish, it seemed, was fundamental. The lights were dimmed. The scent of patchouli was strong. Boredom was my prevailing attitude—shot through at odd intervals with the numinous feeling that somehow anything at all might be possible.

Others seemed less impressed. An attendee identifying himself as a veteran of workshops in human development at the Esalen Institute complained, not without cause, that we’d certainly heard the name Gurdjieff plenty. But what did he teach in specific terms? What did he promise? We’d been told Gurdjieff had answers. I felt my own small disappointment with the session, mired in personal anecdote, without much in the way of a survey of Gurdjieff’s system.

“You’re right to ask,” said one man. “Gurdjieff works by allegory. He says of his writing in All and Everything: ‘I bury the bone so deep that the dogs have to scratch for it.’”

*

The second of Williams’s Gurdjieff stories is titled “George and Susan”; it was published in a 2014 issue of Tin House before appearing in her most recent collection, The Pelican Child. Again Gurdjieff appears on the page initialized as G.—a nod, perhaps, to P. D. Ouspensky’s memoir In Search of the Miraculous, which refers to the teacher only by this initial. In Williams’s story, G. haunts the childhood residence of Susan Sontag in Tucson, where Williams herself lives, and seems possibly to witness a car crash.

Something in Gurdjieff’s travels across state lines at last felt to me to possess the principle of a series. As if sense might be made through dint of sheer repetition. As though there might be a Gurdjieff story for every state in the Union. Why is it that fifty seems more plausible than two? “It is only through effort,” reads one aside in “George and Susan,” “through will, through work work work that two becomes extraordinary.”

This contemplative dimension has always been what I’ve responded to most in Williams’s stories—concerned as they are with their own buried dog bones and esoteric disclosures. Williams’s fiction is full to the brim with prophetic significance, the veiling and unveiling of messages, quasi-theological disputation, revelation of the extraordinary within the everyday, the aleatory coincidence of higher and lower worlds. “The short story,” Williams said on a 1991 episode of KCRW’s Bookworm, “is the closest thing we have to a moral form. It’s a method in which to really dwell upon—reflect upon—the things that matter.”

Perhaps it was Gurdjieff’s own project of dwelling on “the things that matter” that drew Williams to him as a figure in the first place—his belief that these things, forgotten through dint of daily habit, might be again brought to the surface by force of pain or effort.

I think it must have been in the group’s second public meeting that the terms shock and work appeared. Shock meant not as in an emotion, but instead in the shock of experience, necessary to jolt a person from her unawakened life toward the end of finally, hopefully attaining consciousness of herself. Gurdjieff is said at times to have occasioned such shocks by putting his followers in situations of extraordinary discomfort—demanding that they follow impossibly contradictory instructions, dig ditches to the point of exhaustion, and withstand the rageful tirades into which he seemed capable of entering at random.

“I have a proposal,” said one prominent group member who’d introduced himself as an electrical engineer. “A task. Every morning for the next week, I think we should check in with ourselves and exercise gratitude for this moment as well as the day ahead. Would anyone like to take me up on this?”

“I’ll do it.”

“Me too.”

“I can’t wait to.”

Afterward someone approached me to say they’d read “George and Susan” and found it a trip.

*

Meanwhile, my own investigations seemed to have stalled. For some weeks I’d shown up, listened patiently, been honest in my intentions—and all I had to show for my efforts was a list of personal and textual coincidences I found hard to draw meaning from. In my life as a graduate student, two separate faculty mentors for two different reasons directed me toward the same sentence in Edward Said’s On Late Style.

Following up on the indication, I learned that Said’s reference was to Williams’s piece “Hawk,” a personal essay in which she describes sitting down to long hours of piano music during a period of mysterious illness. I was surprised, though I shouldn’t have been, to read her report: “I listened to Thomas de Hartmann play the music of Gurdjieff.” (This hasn’t changed; Williams affirmed as much in an interview with this magazine last year, referring to de Hartmann and Gurdjieff as “her old friends.”)       

I felt compelled to take extraordinary recourse, i.e., violating literary studies’ chief methodological taboo, to never ask an author what she means. I also had a picture postcard featuring a photograph of Jane Bowles that I wanted to send to Williams, whose short fiction is everywhere studded with postcards. “In this world there is a postcard of everything,” says a character in “Train,” a favorite of mine. “That’s the kind of world this is.” How does one select just the right picture for a world in which there’s a postcard of everything? Do we aim to please the recipient? Ourselves? I hoped that my selection of Bowles looking assertive in her unkempt mop top might achieve both. 

But I was uncertain how to ask after the guru Gurdjieff as an enigmatic minor figure in Williams’s corpus—whether in fact there existed a mystical unpublished center around which the two extant stories might be said to orbit. Postcards are, after all, a tricky medium, sent through the mail without an envelope, the handwritten message plain for any postal worker to see. To pose such a question in the plain light of day felt like a gross indelicacy. (“Whence the postcard,” Jacques Derrida writes in The Post Card, “half-private, half-public, neither the one nor the other.”)

My own postcard made it into the mail, at least. Shortly after this I quietly resolved to stop attending the Gurdjieff group. I just couldn’t shake the sense that Gurdjieff’s unique speculative insights had either been intentionally withheld or simply didn’t exist. Which was the worse possibility? It seemed in either case that any answers I sought would remain unforthcoming. Citing a scheduling conflict, I emailed my excuses. In order to awaken, I’d been told, it was first necessary to recognize how one lives in a state of sleep. Maybe I was lacking in mettle to withstand the shock of such an arousal.

*

On the evening of my first missed meeting I awoke with a start to find myself already on the floor by my bedside. The sensation was like jolting from a dream of falling—except that I had in fact fallen. My flinch of automatic reaction came too late and registered instead as a painful, whole-body wince. I made an ugly noise. I thought I’d been concussed. When I put my fingers to my forehead in the dark they came away sticky. A look in the mirror revealed that my partner and I would have to make an early-morning visit to the emergency room.

I was admitted by a pair of drunk attendants and led to a room where I overheard the sounds of another patient’s shoulder being reset over his screams. I answered the nurse’s questions about my injury, stared into his penlight, followed his gloved finger with my eyes. Yes, I’d fallen out of bed—my forehead seemed to have found the vents of my air purifier on the way down, preventing the impact of a more serious drop. The doctor arrived and applied a glue solution he described to me as having an elegant pine scent. Before I knew it I was patched and discharged, awake before the sun, newly billed a $250 copay, sporting over my left eye a fresh wound that I’d been told was little cause for concern so long as I kept it clean.

That very next morning I checked my inbox to find the following from the group member I’d messaged at the outset of my misadventure:

You were missed. Thank you for your email. It is much appreciated. Come next week. The meetings continue. I am in Texas this weekend for a movements intensive. I am very interested in how you are responding to the introductory meetings. Perhaps you tried Robert’s task of taking a moment when your feet hit the floor sitting at the edge of your bed being grateful for life and the day ahead.

In the meantime I became comfortable referring to the resulting mark as my Gurdjieff scar. Or else my Joy Williams scar. I was capable of joking that the spirit of Gurdjieff had given me a bump in the night—and sometimes I even believed it. Mostly I kept quiet, embarrassed that an injury should require so much explanation. Now and then it has occurred to me to wonder whether I have been somehow changed or else humbled, made to recognize the vast stretch of the world beyond the extent of the bounds I’d previously thought known. At minimum, my mailbox was not yet done with me, because that’s when I received my postcard response, on its front a midcentury illustration of poolside vacationers to Palm Springs:

Thanks for the JB card. I don’t have one! Yes, I wanted to do a G collection but my editor at the time, the infamous Gary Fisketjon thought it was nuts. Still—I think—G at the mule dressage events; G at Walden Pond … You should read MAURICE NICOLL and of course OUSPENSKY. Nice hearing from you,

Joy

Drew Dickerson is a writer and graduate student in English at UC Berkeley. His writing has been published in n+1, The Point, The Drift, and The Onion. He is at work on a novel.
